_comment: What this machine was observed to do, per program, merged over the
mechanical part by triage.py so that a new run-all.ps1 run keeps it.
Only entries verified here: a probe's output, a PE header, or the
program's own report line. Anything absent is still to be probed.
Machine: Windows 11 25H2, build 26200.9711, non-admin, no galatest
_notes: run-all.ps1's `fault` field cannot work as written: it reads the Application log's Application Error event (1000), and the runner sets SEM_NOGPFAULTERRORBOX (so crash.exe opens no dialog), which the children inherit and which stops a faulting process reporting to Windows Error Reporting. The log holds no such event from either sweep while holding four older ones, so every entry, crashes included, reads "no Application Error event found". user/windows/fault.py gets the same three facts by debugging the program instead.

Results are not stable between runs on the same machine. Comparing the two sweeps here: com_test 0x6c -> 0x6e, kernel32_system_test 0x58 -> 0x34, security_test 0x21 -> 0x4, pipe_test 0x137 -> 0x14b, process_test 0x47 -> 0x4a, persist_test 0 -> 0x38, tds_test's line went from "first start of the instance". Some of that is tests that keep state across runs (persist_test, tds_test), and some is ordering or timing. A single report does not pin a divergence down.
Only the first failing check of a program is ever known, so fixing one may reveal the next; a count here is of programs, not of divergences.
No test source or binary was changed, as the brief requires. The binaries are cross-compiled on Linux and CI checks user/bin against the sources, and there is no Rust toolchain on this machine.

Some of what a run reports is leftover state rather than a difference: kernel32_file_test fails its first check only because %TEMP%\gala_k32 is still there from the run before. A program that leaves what it made behind reports a different check the second time, so a report is only clean on a clean machine.

Which methods count a check is worked out per test rather than assumed, and has to be: the tests use eq and ok mostly, but also st, ok0, fails and wrappers of their own, the counter is a named field in session_test and a Cell in others, and some methods carry generic parameters. Twelve mappings were wrong before that was handled, registry_test's among them, where the check moved from the ProductName line to the CurrentBuild line and the reported value then made sense.

Round 2 (ROADMAP WD Next item 1): three of the open questions are answered in the entries above, under kernel32_thread_test (SetPriorityClass with mixed values), kernel32_sys_test (WriteConsoleA) and wait_test (NtCreateTimer's unknown type). The user-callback faults and oleaut32_test's and clusapi_test's last call are not: both need the program's own instrumentation, since the fault address is inside ntdll or a system DLL and attributing it to a call would need symbols for our own binaries, which this machine does not have. A fresh run-all.ps1 run is also still to come: the WD fixes are in the sources but user/bin has not been re-exported, so a sweep here would still run the old binaries and report the old checks.

The brief's step 1 was deliberately not done: no galatest account was created and nothing ran elevated. access_test, logon_test and profile_test (ERROR_LOGON_FAILURE), restricted_test (not an administrator) and schannel_test (skipped) are therefore unresolved by choice, not by evidence.

Round 2 sweep, against the binaries exported in 746404e7 (26200.9711): 76 programs exit 0, up from 71, and the entry count fell from 176 to 100 non-zero. All three access violations in our own binaries are gone (dwrite_test and wow64_seh_test now pass; kernel32_sync_test reaches a check instead of faulting), browser_api_test loads, and manifest_test, peb_test and wait_test pass. Seven moved to a later check as expected: kernel32_file_test 1 -> 40, kernel32_sys_test 4 -> 54, kernel32_thread_test 18 -> 36, kuser_test 9 -> 18, registry_test 8 -> 39, sspi_test 21 -> 48, wow64_test 11 -> 71. Nothing regressed. kernel32_file_test moving back to the check it failed on the very first clean run confirms its leftover-state fix. persist_test moved without being re-exported (0x38 -> 0x0e), which is its own state across runs, not a code change.

run-all.ps1 keeps only the first line a program prints that starts with its name, so a program that prints anything informational before failing loses its failure message (quota_test is the case here). Keeping the last such line, or the one carrying "check", would make those diagnosable.

Round 2, second batch (from user/windows/notes-from-linux.md): SetPriorityClass's precedence is answered above and confirms gala's current choice. The other open probe, REALTIME by a process whose token holds SeIncreaseBasePriority disabled, needs an elevated prompt and was not done: elevation was declined for this machine, so it stays open by choice rather than by evidence. run-all.ps1 now keeps the last line a program prints that starts with its name, as asked.

The check-to-line mapping in these entries is counted from the source and is a guess wherever the reported value cannot come from the line it lands on. Five entries are marked so. The tests are being changed to print their own failing line, which removes the guesswork; until then prefer the report line's own "(line L)" where a test gives one.

A correction worth keeping in view: the registry_test finding above was wrong when first reported, because the probe passed a zero-extended predefined key rather than the sign-extended one the x64 SDK defines, and the two behave differently. A probe of a handle-like constant has to use the exact encoding the header produces, and "with a control" did not catch it, since the control was an ordinary opened key rather than the other encoding of the same key.

Round 3 (binaries from 73e727e8, every test printing its failing check's line): kernel32_sync_test, kernel32_sys_test and smpsched_test pass. registry_test moved from check 39 to 100, kernel32_thread_test from 36 to 50, threadinfo_test from 23 back to 14. 68 of 103 entries are mapped from the report's own (line L) and none are counted guesses any more. exit 0 went 76 -> 73, which is the three fixes less bench and the five tcc scripts, all six lost to Defender rather than to code.

A correction: I reported after the first Round 3 attempt that the fixes had had no effect and that the export looked stale. Both were wrong, and from the same cause: that run died on a stderr line before writing windows.json, so I compared the Round 2 report against itself. The three fixes above work. The lesson is to check a report's own timestamp before comparing it, which costs one line.

Round 3 probes (user/windows/round3-analysis.md asked for 19): the five answered so far are gdi32_test, shell32_test, shlwapi_test, sysinfo_test and udp_test, above. run-all.ps1 now also writes every program's whole output to windows-output.txt beside the report, which is what the conpty_test, wow64_k32_test, quota_test and clusapi_test sections asked for ('capture the full stdout') without needing a change to those tests.

Round 3 probes, second batch: com_test and dbghelp_test above, making seven of the nineteen answered (with gdi32_test, shell32_test, shlwapi_test, sysinfo_test and udp_test). The remaining twelve need a window and a message loop (user32_test, controls_test, comctl32_test), a COM server (ole32_test, uia_test), overlapped sockets (winsock_async_test), a 32-bit process (wow64_thread_test), or the program's own instrumentation (quota_test, conpty_test, browser_api_test, wow64_k32_test, clusapi_test), for which windows-output.txt now carries what they print.

Round 3 probes, third batch: controls_test and comctl32_test above, nine of the nineteen answered. The comctl32 one needed care: a probe from Python loads comctl32 version 6 through its manifest, where the FlatSB family returns FALSE for everything, so the first attempt disagreed with the test for a reason that had nothing to do with the question. Loading System32's comctl32 by full path gives version 5 and reproduces the test's own results exactly.

Round 3 probes, fourth batch: user32_test above, ten of the nineteen answered. It took two attempts worth noting: the hook callback first declared lParam signed, so CallNextHookEx raised on every notification and the hook chain was never continued. The counts happened to be right anyway, but the run was not trustworthy until the signature was fixed and it was repeated.

Round 3 probes, fifth batch: ole32_test above, eleven of the nineteen answered. It is worth recording how it was found: the first probe copied the test exactly and got E_INVALIDARG, which said nothing; the single-interface call in the same run happened to pass pItf=NULL and succeeded, and running the three-interface call both ways isolated pItf as the whole difference.

Round 4 (binaries from f0102817, runner from c650ada0): 93 programs exit 0, up from 73, and nothing that passed now fails. Twenty newly pass, com_test and sysinfo_test among them, both from probes here. oleaut32_test no longer crashes and reaches check 108. Twenty-seven moved to a later check, several a long way: wow64_test 71 -> 1478, user32_test 42 -> 134, kernel32_clr_test 10 -> 132. bench ran this time rather than being quarantined. The five tcc-dependent scripts still fail, still Defender. The sweep ran before the Linux gate had declared the export green, so it may need repeating.
Round 4's four new probes (notes-from-linux, "New probes, from the fixes"), all measured here on 26200.9711:

1. RtlRaiseException called directly, with ExceptionFlags 0 in the record passed in: the handler sees ExceptionFlags 0x80 (EXCEPTION_SOFTWARE_ORIGINATE). RaiseException gives exactly the same, so the flag is not something RaiseException adds on the way past; it is set for a software-raised exception either way. Probed with a vectored handler in a child process, reading the EXCEPTION_RECORD it is given, with code 0x0e0abcde and no parameters.

2. A PE32+ image mapped away from its preferred base: the mapped OptionalHeader.ImageBase is rewritten to the address it was actually mapped at, exactly as the PE32 case in wow64_import_test. kernel32.dll, ntdll.dll and advapi32.dll all read 0x180000000 in the file and their real load address in memory.

3. A PE32 image mapped as a section in this 64-bit process: NtMapViewOfSection returns STATUS_IMAGE_MACHINE_TYPE_MISMATCH (0x4000000e), and it returns that whether the preferred base is free or taken. Probed with SysWOW64's kernel32.dll and user/bin's testkernel32_32.dll, both preferring 0x10000000, first with that address free and then with it reserved: 0x4000000e both times, and the view still mapped (at 0x74c50000 and 0x690000). So the machine-type status wins over STATUS_IMAGE_NOT_AT_BASE rather than the two combining, and neither is a failure.

4. PeekNamedPipe on a byte-mode pipe holding 5 bytes: lpBytesLeftThisMessage is not a constant 0xffffffff but the negative of what was read. With a 1-byte buffer it is 0xffffffff (-1) and lpBytesRead 1; with a 5-byte buffer it is 0xfffffffb (-5) and lpBytesRead 5; with lpBuffer NULL it is 0 and lpBytesRead 0. lpTotalBytesAvail is 5 in every case and the call returns TRUE. A byte-mode pipe has no messages, so the field comes out as 0 minus the bytes taken.

A correction to this triage's own output, after the Linux side reported that triage.md's asserts: quoted a neighbouring line in about ten entries. It was nineteen of fifty-one, and the cause was mine: triage.py read the test sources from the working tree while the report came from binaries built at an older commit, so every line the fixes had moved came out wrong. It now takes --sources, pointed at the tree the binaries were built from, which brings it to fifty-two exact and two that still do not look like checks. It also searches a test's other .c files, since shlwapi_test is main.c plus the url.c it includes; where the same line number holds a check in both, the entry says so and names each instead of choosing, which is the case for shlwapi_test's line 242.

Round 4's probes, first batch: kernel32_system_test, shlwapi_test, ole32_test, controls_test, gdi32_test and shell32_test above, six of the twelve the analysis marks. The VerSetConditionMask one is worth reading for its own sake: the report said "got 0x18", which is exactly what the check asserts, because the test prints 32 bits of a 64-bit value and the difference is in bit 63.

kernel32_thread_test.windows: SetPriorityClass does not validate the value as a whole: it takes the recognised class bits out of it and the lowest class wins, IDLE first. A value carrying at least one recognised bit succeeds; a nonzero value carrying none is refused like 0, with FALSE and ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER (87). REALTIME (0x100) returns TRUE but leaves the class at HIGH (0x80) without SeIncreaseBasePriorityPrivilege. The precedence among the recognised bits is a strict order, and it is the inverse of scheduling priority: the lowest class always wins. Over all fifteen pairs, IDLE beats all five others, BELOW_NORMAL four, NORMAL three, ABOVE_NORMAL two, HIGH one, and REALTIME none.
kernel32_thread_test.evidence: probed here, resetting to NORMAL between calls. Recognised alone: 0x20->0x20, 0x40->0x40, 0x80->0x80, 0x4000->0x4000, 0x8000->0x8000, 0x100->1 err=0 but class 0x80. IDLE wins over the rest: 0x60, 0xc0, 0x140, 0x4040 all -> 0x40. 0x12345 (has 0x40 and 0x100) -> 0x40, and 0x12305, the same value with 0x40 cleared, -> 0x80 through its 0x100. No recognised bit: 0x1, 0x2, 0x8, 0x10, 0x200, 0x1000, 0x10000 all -> 0 err=87. Round 2, every pair probed: 0x4020 and 0x4080 -> BELOW_NORMAL, 0x8020 -> NORMAL, 0x8080 -> ABOVE_NORMAL, 0xa0 and 0x120 -> NORMAL, 0x180 -> HIGH, 0x4100 -> BELOW_NORMAL, 0x8100 -> ABOVE_NORMAL, 0xc000 -> BELOW_NORMAL, and every pair containing IDLE -> IDLE.
kernel32_thread_test.note: A real divergence, and the rule is not the one it first looks like: it is not that the IDLE bit means IDLE, but that unrecognised bits are ignored while any recognised one decides, with IDLE taking precedence. So an unknown value is refused when it carries no class bit at all, which means gala cannot simply accept every nonzero value either. The REALTIME downgrade is a second, separate thing to match. Round 2, from ROADMAP WD Next item 1. So the Linux side's "gala takes the lowest class for now" is already right, and the test can assert it. Answers the open probe for two class bits with neither being IDLE's. Round 3: the tests now print their own failing line, so the mapping is exact and no longer counted.

registry_test.note: CORRECTION of what this entry said before. My first probe passed only the zero-extended value and I generalised it to "predefined keys fail", concluding the test's comment was wrong and that gala closing them successfully was wrong too. gdi32_test.windows: Segoe UI at lfHeight -12 on a CreateDC("DISPLAY") at 96 DPI measures tmHeight 15, tmAscent 12, tmDescent 3, tmInternalLeading 3, tmExternalLeading 0.
gdi32_test.evidence: probed here, recording all five metrics the analysis asked for, with GetDeviceCaps(LOGPIXELSY) = 96 to fix the DPI the numbers belong to.
gdi32_test.note: The test wants tmHeight 16 and tmAscent 13, so both are one less here while tmDescent agrees. Worth noting for whoever fixes it that these depend on the DPI, so the test should either pin the DPI it assumes or derive the numbers from the font it asked for.

shell32_test.windows: ExtractIconW(NULL, <a plain .txt file>, 0) returns NULL with GetLastError 0, for a relative name and for an absolute path alike.
shell32_test.evidence: probed here against a .txt file created for the purpose, from its own directory and by full path.
shell32_test.note: The documented 1 for a file that is not an executable, DLL or icon does not hold on this build: it returns no handle at all and sets no error. The test asserts (HICON)1.

shlwapi_test.windows: AssocQueryStringW with a 4-character buffer returns 0x8007007a (ERROR_INSUFFICIENT_BUFFER as an HRESULT), not E_POINTER. It sets the length to what is needed (32 for .galatest, 108 for .txt) and it does write into the buffer, truncated: the four characters come back as '"C:' and a NUL, not untouched.
shlwapi_test.evidence: probed here with ASSOCSTR_COMMAND for .galatest and for .txt as a control, recording the HRESULT, the length after the call and the buffer's contents, as the analysis asked.
shlwapi_test.note: Two differences in one check: the status is the insufficient-buffer one rather than E_POINTER, and the buffer is written rather than left alone. The length behaving as the test expects is the half that holds.

sysinfo_test.windows: NtQuerySystemInformation(124, SystemQueryPerformanceCounterInformation) needs its Version field pre-filled with 1 in the input buffer. Without it the call returns STATUS_NOT_SUPPORTED whatever the buffer size; with it, it succeeds and returns 12 bytes.
sysinfo_test.evidence: probed here at sizes 8, 12, 16 and 24, with and without Version=1. Without: 0xc00000bb at every size. With: 0 at 12, 16 and 24, returning 12 bytes, 01000000 00000000 01000000.
sysinfo_test.note: This answers the probe exactly: the status is about the input, not the length. The test passes a 12-byte buffer it has not filled in, so it must set Version=1 first.

udp_test.windows: setsockopt(SO_RANDOMIZE_PORT) succeeds on an unbound UDP socket and fails on a bound one with WSAEINVAL (10022). The option has to be set before bind.
udp_test.evidence: probed here on two UDP sockets, one bound to 0.0.0.0:0 and one untouched.
udp_test.note: A real divergence in ordering rather than in the option: the test sets it on an already-bound socket. The 0xffffffff it reported is setsockopt's -1.

com_test.windows: SafeArrayAllocDescriptorEx(VT_I4, 1) succeeds and sets fFeatures to 0x0080 (FADF_HAVEVARTYPE) with the VARTYPE 3 in the four bytes before the descriptor, but leaves cbElements at 0. SafeArrayAllocData then succeeds and gives a non-NULL pvData, and cbElements is still 0. SafeArrayGetVartype reads VT_I4 back correctly.
com_test.evidence: probed here, recording cbElements, fFeatures, the VARTYPE at -4 and pvData after each call, as the analysis asked.
com_test.note: A real divergence, and a narrow one: of the two things check 110 asserts, pvData != NULL holds and cbElements == 4 does not. This build does not derive the element size from the VARTYPE, so SafeArrayAllocData allocated three elements of zero bytes. gala filling cbElements in is the wrong half to keep.

dbghelp_test.windows: SymSrvGetFileIndexInfoW fails with ERROR_BAD_EXE_FORMAT (193) on an image that has no debug directory, and succeeds on one that has any entry at all. It also requires sizeofstruct to be exactly 1608; 1604, 1607, 1609, 0 and 4096 all give ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER.
dbghelp_test.evidence: probed here. dbghelp_test.exe and user32_test.exe, both C tests, have an empty debug directory (rva 0, size 0) and fail with 193. commit_test.exe has one 28-byte entry, the single IMAGE_DEBUG_DIRECTORY that /Brepro writes, and succeeds; so do kernel32.dll (112 bytes of entries) and an ordinary python.exe. The test's own struct is the documented one and does come to 1608, so sizeofstruct is not the problem here.
dbghelp_test.note: The test calls it on its own file, which is the one case that cannot work: the C tests are built by user/<test>/build.sh without /Brepro, so they carry no debug directory, while the Rust tests get one from the linker flags in .cargo/config.toml. Either give the C builds a debug directory or have the test ask about a file that has one. Not a divergence in the API.

controls_test.windows: CB_RESETCONTENT returns 1, not CB_OKAY (0). CB_GETCOUNT afterwards returns 0, as the test expects.
controls_test.evidence: probed here on a CBS_DROPDOWNLIST combo with three items, recording the two return values separately.
controls_test.note: The documented "the return value is always CB_OKAY" does not hold on this build. Half the check is right: the list is emptied. This is the second time a controls_test check has been half right in the same way, the earlier one being CB_SETCURSEL past the end.

comctl32_test.windows: FlatSB_GetScrollProp(WSB_PROP_WINSTYLE) returns the window's WS_*SCROLL bits plus one low bit per scroll bar: 0x2 for vertical, 0x4 for horizontal. For a WS_VSCROLL-only window, which is what the test creates, it returns 0x00200002 rather than WS_VSCROLL's 0x00200000.
comctl32_test.evidence: probed here against comctl32 5.82.26100.8328, loaded by full path. WS_VSCROLL only -> 0x00200002; WS_HSCROLL only -> 0x00100004; both -> 0x00300006; neither -> 0. The other properties the test sets read back exactly: VSTYLE 0, CXVSCROLL 21, VBKGCOLOR 0x00030201.
comctl32_test.note: A real divergence, and a one-bit one: the test asserts v == WS_VSCROLL and should mask or expect the extra bit. Also worth knowing for anyone probing this: in a process that activates comctl32 version 6, every FlatSB_GetScrollProp returns FALSE and leaves the output untouched, so the whole family has to be probed against version 5, which is what a test without a manifest gets.

user32_test.windows: One CreateWindowExW raises HCBT_CREATEWND twice when the new window is the first in its thread: once for the window itself and once for the thread's default IME window, class "IME", title "Default IME". With a window already created in the thread it fires once.
user32_test.evidence: probed here with a WH_CBT hook on the current thread, logging each HCBT_CREATEWND's hwnd, GetClassNameW and the CREATESTRUCT's title, as the analysis asked. First window in the thread: [('ProbeB','hooked'), ('IME','Default IME')]. With one window made beforehand: [('ProbeB','hooked')].
user32_test.note: A real divergence that the test can absorb: check 42 asserts cbt_creates == 1, and the hooked window is the thread's first, so Windows makes the IME window inside the same call and the hook counts two. gala presumably creates no IME window, which is why it passes there. The test can create a throwaway window before installing the hook, ignore HCBT_CREATEWND for class "IME", or count the window it asked for rather than the calls.

ole32_test.windows: CoCreateInstanceEx with one valid MULTI_QI (pItf NULL) and one invalid (pItf non-NULL) returns E_INVALIDARG, and it does not leave the array alone: the first entry comes back hr E_NOINTERFACE with pItf NULL, and the second is untouched, still hr 7 and pItf 1.
ole32_test.evidence: probed here with {IUnknown, NULL, 7} and {IUIAutomation, (IUnknown*)1, 7}, recording each entry's hr and pItf as the analysis asked.
ole32_test.note: So the entries are processed in order and the one that is already filled in is abandoned where it stands, rather than the whole array being validated first. The E_INVALIDARG the test asserts is right; what it can expect of the entries afterwards is this.

conpty_test.windows: The child starts but its standard handles are not console handles: it prints "child: not a console, error 6" (ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE). The pseudo console's output pipe carries only two escape sequences, [?9001h and [?1004h (win32 input mode and focus events), and never the child's "ready".
conpty_test.evidence: the program's whole output, now kept in windows-output.txt: "child started", then "child: not a console, error 6", then "output was: [?9001h[?1004h", then check 4 failing after the full 20 s wait (20063 ms).
conpty_test.note: Answers the probe without changing the test. The child is attached to the pseudo console but its handles do not answer as a console here, so the 20 s wait was never going to end. The two sequences are what conhost emits on attach, so the console side came up; it is the child's handles that differ.

wow64_k32_test.windows: check 28 fails at line 207 (0xcf) with 0x73, that is 115.
wow64_k32_test.evidence: the program's own line, now kept in windows-output.txt: "(line 0x000000cf) wow64_k32_test: check 0000001c failed, got 00000073". It also prints "hello" first, which is why the report used to show that instead.
wow64_k32_test.note: The counted mapping in the analysis was right: line 207 is the GetSystemDirectoryW check. The value 115 is what the call returned where the test wants the length of C:\Windows\SysWOW64. Whether 115 is a length or a status is for whoever reads line 207; nothing more can be told from outside.

kernel32_system_test.windows: VerSetConditionMask(0, VER_MAJORVERSION, VER_GREATER_EQUAL) returns 0x8000000000000018, not 0x18: bit 63 is set as well as the condition. (0, VER_MINORVERSION, VER_EQUAL) gives 0x8000000000000001 and (0, VER_BUILDNUMBER, VER_LESS) gives 0x8000000000000100, so the high bit is there every time.
kernel32_system_test.evidence: probed here for all three combinations the analysis asked for.
kernel32_system_test.note: This also explains the report line, which read "got 0x18" and so looked as though it matched: the test prints the low 32 bits of a u64, and those are 0x18 exactly as asserted, while the comparison sees bit 63 too. Whoever fixes the test should mask or expect that bit, and printing the full u64 would have made the failure readable.
